clinicalPearls: Reduced target-tissue responsiveness to thyroid hormone, most often from dominant-negative mutations in THRB, the gene for the beta isoform of the thyroid hormone receptor.
The hallmark biochemistry is elevated free thyroid hormones with an unsuppressed — normal or mildly raised — thyroid-stimulating hormone.
The clinical picture is variable; many patients are compensated and euthyroid, but hypothyroid and thyrotoxic features can coexist in different tissues.
Goitre is common, and tachycardia or attention and learning difficulties may occur because alpha-receptor-rich tissues such as the heart remain responsive.
The principal differential is a thyroid-stimulating-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma, which produces a similar biochemical pattern.
Distinguishing tests include the alpha subunit, sex-hormone-binding globulin, a thyrotrophin-releasing hormone stimulation test and genetic and family studies.
Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, and screening relatives frequently reveals others with the same biochemistry.
Most patients need no treatment, and inappropriate anti-thyroid therapy or gland ablation can be harmful.
reference.pathophysiology: Refetoff syndrome reflects reduced end-organ responsiveness to thyroid hormone, most often caused by heterozygous mutations in THRB encoding the beta isoform of the thyroid hormone receptor. Mutant receptors bind triiodothyronine poorly or fail to regulate transcription and exert a dominant-negative effect over the normal allele. Because the hypothalamus and pituitary depend on the beta receptor for negative feedback, thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion is not appropriately suppressed by the high circulating free thyroxine and triiodothyronine, producing the characteristic pattern of elevated free thyroid hormones with a normal or even raised thyroid-stimulating hormone. Tissues in which the alpha receptor isoform predominates — notably the heart, and parts of the central nervous system and bone — remain responsive to the high hormone levels, so patients can simultaneously display hypothyroid features in beta-dependent tissues and thyrotoxic features such as tachycardia in alpha-dependent tissues, accounting for the variable, tissue-selective phenotype. A rare recessive form due to complete THRB loss was described in the original consanguineous kindred, associated with deaf-mutism and stippled epiphyses.
additionalDifferentials: Laboratory assay interference from heterophile antibodies, biotin or anti-iodothyronine antibodies

Thyroid hormone cell-membrane transporter defect (MCT8, Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome)
Thyroid hormone metabolism defect from selenocysteine insertion sequence-binding protein 2 mutation
additionalInvestigations: Free thyroxine, free triiodothyronine and thyroid-stimulating hormone, with confirmatory repeat testing
Alpha subunit and the alpha-subunit-to-thyroid-stimulating-hormone molar ratio, raised in a secreting adenoma
Sex-hormone-binding globulin, typically normal in resistance but high in true thyrotoxicosis
Thyrotrophin-releasing hormone stimulation test, with a preserved response favouring resistance
Pituitary MRI to exclude a secreting adenoma
THRB gene sequencing and biochemical screening of relatives
redFlags: A pituitary mass with headache or visual field defect, favouring a secreting adenoma over resistance
Cardiac arrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation, or heart failure, from thyrotoxic tissue effects
Growth or developmental concerns in an affected child
Iatrogenic thyroid ablation performed on a misdiagnosis, leaving management difficult
reference.prognosis: With correct recognition and either no treatment or careful, individualised management the outlook is generally good and lifespan normal. Most morbidity stems from misdiagnosis with inappropriate anti-thyroid treatment or from tissue-selective thyrotoxic effects.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as Graves disease and giving anti-thyroid drugs, radioiodine or thyroidectomy.
Failing to exclude a thyroid-stimulating-hormone-secreting adenoma before labelling the picture as resistance.
Overlooking laboratory assay interference as the explanation for the biochemistry.
Treating the numbers rather than the patient, when most individuals are compensated and euthyroid.
management: Recognise the diagnosis to avoid inappropriate anti-thyroid drugs or thyroid ablation for the raised free thyroid hormones
Manage many compensated, euthyroid patients with monitoring alone, as tissue resistance is offset by the high circulating hormone
Use beta-blockade to control tachycardia and adrenergic symptoms arising from responsive alpha-receptor-rich tissues such as the heart

Distinguish resistance from a thyroid-stimulating-hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma before treating, using the alpha subunit, sex-hormone-binding globulin, a thyrotrophin-releasing hormone stimulation test and pituitary MRI
Give careful, individualised thyroid hormone supplementation only where hypothyroid features or growth and developmental concerns predominate
Monitor goitre, cardiac status, growth and neurodevelopment, and offer genetic testing with biochemical screening and counselling of relatives
